title: The Enlightenment in Europe
summary: The Enlightenment was a revolution in thought in Europe and North America from the late 17th to the late 18th century. Its writers used reason to challenge knowledge based on faith and superstition, and called for individual liberty and religious toleration. Its heart lay among the French philosophes, including Voltaire, Montesquieu and Diderot, whose Encyclopedia became its central work. It is often associated with political revolutions, especially the French Revolution of 1789.

uncertainty.note: Dated variously from c. 1685 (or 1700) to 1789 (the outbreak of the French Revolution) or 1815 (the close of the Napoleonic Wars).

as_recorded.value: European politics, philosophy, science and communications were radically reoriented during the course of the “long 18th century” (1685-1815) as part of a movement referred to by its participants as the Age of Reason, or simply the Enlightenment.
The Enlightenment is usually dated from the last quarter of the 17th century to the last quarter of the 18th century.
The heart of the eighteenth century Enlightenment is the loosely organized activity of prominent French thinkers of the mid-decades of the eighteenth century, the so-called “philosophes”

where.historical_name: Paris, Kingdom of France (intellectual capital of the Enlightenment philosophes)

importance.justification: Made reason, liberty and toleration central ideals of modern thought and politics.

reviewer_note: Dates vary: one source uses a long 18th century of 1685–1815, while this record ends at 1789. The pin is Paris, home of the philosophes, as a proxy for a movement across two continents.
